node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mean as balance point
node.description: Interpret the mean as a balancing or fair-share value for a numerical data set.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Calculate mean
node.description: Calculate the mean by adding values and dividing by the number of values.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Median of ordered data
node.description: Find the median by ordering data and locating the middle value or middle pair.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mode as most frequent value
node.description: Identify the mode as the value or category that occurs most often.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Choose measure of centre
node.description: Choose mean, median or mode to summarise a data set based on data type and context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Effect of outliers on centre
node.description: Describe how outliers can affect mean, median and mode differently.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Centre in context
node.description: Interpret a measure of centre as a typical value in the context of the data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Range as spread
node.description: Use the range to describe the distance between the smallest and largest data values.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Deviations from centre
node.description: Describe how data values vary from a typical or central value.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Quartiles introduction
node.description: Use quartiles to divide ordered data into four approximately equal parts.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interquartile range
node.description: Calculate and interpret the interquartile range as the spread of the middle half of the data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Five-number summary
node.description: Summarise data using minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outliers using context
node.description: Identify and interpret possible outliers using both data values and context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Variability in repeated data
node.description: Recognise that repeated measurements, samples or trials can vary naturally.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare centres
node.description: Compare groups or distributions using appropriate measures of centre.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare spreads
node.description: Compare groups or distributions using range, interquartile range or visual spread.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare shapes of distributions
node.description: Compare distributions by describing symmetry, skew, peaks, clusters and gaps.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare outliers
node.description: Compare distributions by considering possible outliers and their effects on interpretation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare two dot plots
node.description: Compare two dot plots using centre, spread, shape and unusual values.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare box plots
node.description: Compare two or more box plots using median, quartiles, spread and outliers.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Statistical claims from distributions
node.description: Make cautious claims about groups using distribution comparisons and context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mean is sensitive to extremes
node.description: Very large or very small values can pull the mean toward them.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Median needs ordered data
node.description: The median is found after values are placed in order.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mode is most frequent
node.description: The mode is the value or category that appears most often, and there may be no mode or multiple modes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Centre describes typical value
node.description: A measure of centre summarises what is typical for a data set, but different centres answer different questions.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Range uses maximum and minimum
node.description: The range is the maximum value minus the minimum value.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: IQR describes middle half
node.description: The interquartile range describes the spread of the middle half of ordered data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outliers are unusual values
node.description: Outliers are values that are unusually far from the rest of the data and need contextual interpretation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare distributions using multiple features
node.description: Distribution comparison should consider centre, spread, shape, outliers and context together.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Context controls summary interpretation
node.description: The same summary statistic can mean different things depending on what the data describe.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Variability is expected
node.description: Data values often vary naturally across people, objects, measurements, samples or trials.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mean always best centre
node.description: Learner assumes the mean is always the best summary of typical value, even with skewed data or outliers.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Median from unsorted middle position
node.description: Learner chooses the middle listed value without first ordering the data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Range describes all variation
node.description: Learner treats the range as a complete description of spread and ignores how values are distributed between the extremes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outlier always error
node.description: Learner assumes every outlier must be a mistake rather than a value requiring investigation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare only by centre
node.description: Learner compares distributions only by mean or median and ignores spread, shape, outliers and context.

edge.rationale: Mean as a balance or fair-share value is a core interpretation of centre.
Calculating mean is a central measure-of-centre skill.
Median is a central measure of centre for ordered numerical data.
Mode is a common centre or typicality summary for categorical and discrete data.
Choosing among measures of centre is an important summary-statistics decision.
Outliers affect interpretation and choice of centre.
Measures of centre must be interpreted in context.
Range is an introductory measure of spread.
Deviations from centre support reasoning about variability.
Quartiles support later IQR and box-plot interpretation.
Interquartile range is a core measure of spread for the middle half of data.
Five-number summaries describe centre and spread together.
Outliers are a key feature of variation and spread interpretation.
Repeated data variability supports the idea that data naturally vary.
Comparing centres is a core part of comparing distributions.
Comparing spreads is a core part of comparing distributions.
Distribution shape is a major comparison feature.
Outliers can change distribution comparisons and interpretations.
Comparing dot plots directly practises visual distribution comparison.
Comparing box plots practises summary-based distribution comparison.
Distribution comparisons support cautious statistical claims in context.
Mean as balance is easier to interpret from organised numerical data displays.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats mean only as a procedure and not as a summary of data values.

edge.rationale: Calculating mean should connect to mean as a fair-share or balance value.
edge.failure_signal: Learner follows the algorithm but cannot interpret the result as a typical value.

edge.rationale: Median requires locating ordered numerical data values.
edge.failure_signal: Learner selects the middle listed value without ordering the data.

edge.rationale: Mode depends on identifying the most frequent value or category.
edge.failure_signal: Learner confuses highest value with most frequent value.

edge.rationale: Choosing a measure of centre requires knowing how at least mean and median summarise data.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses mean by default regardless of data type or outliers.

edge.rationale: Understanding outlier effects helps explain why different centres may be chosen.
edge.failure_signal: Learner does not notice that an extreme value changes the mean more than the median.

edge.rationale: Interpreting centre in context requires choosing and understanding the summary statistic.
edge.failure_signal: Learner reports a number without explaining what it means in context.

edge.rationale: Spread is introduced alongside centre to describe more than a typical value.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares only typical values and ignores how far data vary.

edge.rationale: Deviations from centre extend basic spread reasoning beyond minimum and maximum.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot describe how far values are from a typical value.

edge.rationale: Quartiles require ordering data and locating middle positions in halves of the data.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot locate quartiles consistently in ordered data.

edge.rationale: Interquartile range is calculated from the first and third quartiles.
edge.failure_signal: Learner subtracts unrelated values rather than Q3 minus Q1.

edge.rationale: Five-number summaries combine extremes, median and quartiles.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot identify the ordered summary values needed for a box plot.

edge.rationale: Outliers are recognised by comparing values to the overall distribution pattern and context.
edge.failure_signal: Learner labels any largest value as an outlier without considering context or pattern.

edge.rationale: Reasoning about repeated-data variability requires understanding that collected data can vary across repeated observations or trials.
edge.failure_signal: Learner expects repeated measurements or trials to always produce identical values.

edge.rationale: Comparing centres requires interpreting centre summaries in context for each group.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares mean or median values without interpreting what they represent.

edge.rationale: Comparing spreads uses range, IQR or visual spread between distributions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares groups by centre only and ignores variability.

edge.rationale: Comparing shapes requires recognising distribution shape features in displays.
edge.failure_signal: Learner describes individual points but not overall distribution shape.

edge.rationale: Comparing outliers builds from identifying and interpreting outliers within one distribution.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats unusual values as irrelevant or always erroneous.

edge.rationale: Comparing dot plots uses centre along with visual spread and shape features.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares displays by one visible point rather than the distribution.

edge.rationale: Comparing box plots requires reading medians, quartiles, whiskers and ranges.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares box lengths or positions without interpreting the five-number summary.

edge.rationale: Making statistical claims from distributions requires comparing centre, spread, shape and context.
edge.failure_signal: Learner overstates a conclusion from a single statistic or display feature.
